measuring: Slope is always written rise/run with run fixed at 12 — 6" of rise per foot is 6/12.
Below 4/12 manufacturers require special low-slope underlayment procedures; 2/12 is the absolute floor for shingles.
Level out 12", measure straight up to the rafter — that vertical distance is the rise per foot of run.
The square (100 sq ft) is the unit all roofing material and labor is priced in.
Overhangs are real roof surface that floor plans miss — measure to the drip edge.
It's the hypotenuse of a 12-unit run and the rise, divided back by 12.
Net area is what you actually cover — big openings come out, small penetrations ride in waste.
A hip or valley slopes in two directions at once, so its true length beats its plan length.
The hips consume half the width at each end, shortening the ridge by the full building width.
More valleys, dormers and cuts = more offcuts you can't reuse — waste climbs past 15%.
sheathing: Tile adds 3–4× the dead load of asphalt — an engineer must confirm the framing first.
A sagging ridge means the structure or sheathing below has failed or was undersized.
Backed-up gutters soak the fascia and deck edge first — that's where rot begins.
Staggered joints spread weak points; the 1/8" gap absorbs panel swelling.
H-clips stiffen panel edges that don't land on a rafter, preventing sag between supports.
Wood shingles and shakes must dry from below — the gaps let the deck breathe.
6" at panel edges, 12" in the field is the standard baseline schedule.
4 × 8 = 32 sq ft per panel — the divisor for every decking takeoff.
You can't see rot until tear-off, so the contract prices it per sheet in advance.
Spreading the load along framing near the ridge avoids point-loading a span.
underlayment: Synthetics out-perform felt on strength, weight and UV life — that's why they took over.
The rubberized asphalt flows around the fastener shank, sealing every nail hole.
Metal panels run hot — standard membrane can soften and flow; high-temp smooth stock doesn't.
Ice dams push water uphill; membrane must reach 24" inside the heated wall line to stay ahead of it.
Roofing is shingled downhill — every upper layer must lap over the one below it.
End (side) laps take 6" because vertical seams are the vulnerable ones.
Low slope drains slowly, so shingles there need two layers of protection beneath.
Weather doesn't check the schedule — never expose more deck than you can dry-in today.
A No. 15 roll is ~4 squares; that number drives the dry-in order.
It's applied in strips at eaves, valleys and penetrations — so it's measured in lineal feet.
One L-piece woven into every course keeps each course's water on top of the flashing below.
Counterflashing caps the assembly so water can't sneak behind the step flashing's top edge.
A cricket splits the water around the high side of a wide chimney instead of letting it pool.
Neoprene boots sun-rot in 10–15 years — long before the shingles around them fail.
Old flashing carries old fatigue and old leak paths into your brand-new roof.
asphalt: Laminated (architectural) shingles are the market standard — better wind ratings and looks than 3-tab.
UL 2218 Class 4 is the top impact rating, and many insurers discount premiums for it.
Granule color varies slightly between production lots — mixed lots show as banding.
Four nails per shingle is the standard schedule; six is for high-wind or steep work.
High nails miss the top edge of the course below, so each shingle holds only itself.
Rakes need starter too — the edge sealant line is what stops edge lift in wind.
Nails near the centerline puncture the waterway where the most water runs.
Sealant strips need heat to bond; cold installs may need hand-sealing with cement.
Standard laminates package 3 bundles to the square — confirm on the wrapper.
Figure ~300 lbs per square per layer when sizing dumpsters and pricing disposal.
Starter, caps and disposal are the most-missed lines — and about a tenth of job cost.
rollroofing: Rolls are 36" × ~36' — right at one square before lap losses.
It's an honest 8–12 year economy cover — sell it as exactly that.
The 18"-under, 36"-over cemented pair is the classic valley lining detail.
Half of each course is covered by the next, giving two layers everywhere water goes.
Concealed nails sit under cemented laps, protected from weather and backout.
6" staggered, cemented end laps keep the vertical joints watertight.
Half the roll becomes overlap, so net coverage halves and the roll count doubles.
Widths that fight the 36" module strip-waste every course — raise the waste factor.
Cold asphalt cracks — warm rolls relax flat and lay without splitting.
wood: Shakes are split for texture; shingles are sawn smooth both faces for tight tolerances.
Roof-grade cedar is No. 1 Blue Label: all clear, all edge-grain, all heartwood.
Many wildfire jurisdictions restrict or ban untreated wood roofs — check before quoting.
Two nails let the wood move; more nails split it as it swells and shrinks.
The felt interlay blocks wind-driven water in the thick open keyways between shakes.
Wood swells with moisture — keyways give each piece room to grow.
Trapped moisture rots wood roofs; both faces must be able to dry.
Coverage is rated at a standard exposure — run it wider or tighter and coverage shifts.
Every piece is hand-placed and gauged — cedar labor runs 2–3× asphalt hours.
tile: Standard tile runs 600–1,100+ lbs per square — a structural conversation, not a shingle swap.
Fired clay holds its color for a century; concrete color can soften over decades.
Tiles crack mid-span — step on the supported headlap areas or foam pads.
Tile sheds water; the underlayment beneath is the actual waterproof layer.
Bird stops close the arched openings at the eave so birds and embers stay out.
The tile outlives the felt — lift it, re-paper, and relay the same tile.
Wind can't be allowed to peel tile — foam, clips or extra fasteners hold the edge zones.
Tiles-per-square varies by profile — the data sheet, not memory, sets the count.
Handling and foot traffic break a few percent — order the allowance up front.
slate: ASTM S1 is the top grade — 75+ year service expectancy from the best quarries.
S1 stone outlasts cheap metal — copper and stainless are the only fasteners that keep up.
Slate hangs on its nails; driving them tight cracks the stone as the roof moves.
There's no sealant in a slate roof — the headlap overlap is the waterproofing.
The ripper slides under the slate and hooks the hidden nails to cut them.
The stone is usually fine at 90 years — it's the fasteners and flashings that quit.
Half of what isn't headlap shows: exposure = (length − headlap) ÷ 2.
Brittle stone plus handling equals breakage — 3–5% is the working allowance.
You walk the staging and ladders, never the stone — slate breaks underfoot.
metal: Concealed clips eliminate face holes and let panels float with temperature.
The mechanically folded double-lock seam is watertight enough for near-flat slopes.
Gauge runs backwards — 24 gauge is thicker and stronger than 29.
PVDF (Kynar) resists fade and chalk far longer than polyester paints.
Oil-canning is cosmetic waviness in flat pans — control it with striations and gauge.
Copper is nobler than steel — its runoff eats the steel panel galvanically.
Butyl tape stays elastic hidden in the lap; exposed caulk beads fail in the sun.
Panel temperatures cook standard membranes — high-temp underlayment only.
Panels come cut to length, so you count widths across the eave, not squares.
Every trim profile — ridge, rake, eave, valley — is its own lineal-foot line item.
lowslope: BUR is built on site from alternating felt plies and bitumen moppings.
Each ply is another complete water barrier — four plies, four chances.
Moppings run 20–25 lbs/sq each, plus a ~60 lb flood coat under gravel.
APP is the torch-grade modifier — the flame fuses it to the substrate.
Self-adhered SBS needs no flame — the safe choice over occupied homes.
Smoldering starts hide in cavities — the post-torch fire watch is non-negotiable.
The 48-hour standard separates normal drying from true ponding.
1/4" per foot is the minimum designed drainage for 'flat' roofs.
You fix ponding by rebuilding slope — tapered insulation, crickets, or more drains.
singleply: PVC's chemistry shrugs off grease and chemicals — the restaurant-roof membrane.
EPDM is thermoset rubber — it can't be heat-welded, so seams are taped/glued on primer.
The mil thickness above the scrim is the wear layer — that's the quality number.
TPO and PVC are different plastics that won't fuse — never mix their accessories.
Mechanically attached rows of plates in the laps hold the sheet; the field floats.
Weld temperature and speed drift with the weather — prove the settings every morning.
River rock is real load — ballast requires verified structure and low wind-debris exposure.
Details — corners, boots, terminations — are their own takeoff on every membrane job.
Uplift is strongest at corners and perimeter — attachment is enhanced there by design.
insulation: R-value is thermal resistance — the higher the number, the slower the heat loss.
Polyiso's ~R-6 per inch makes it the flat-roof insulation workhorse.
Tapered systems build drainage slope into dead-flat decks.
Fill jammed in the eaves chokes intake air — baffles keep the soffit path open.
Vapor drives toward cold; the retarder goes on the warm side to stop it early.
Air leaks move far more moisture than diffusion — seal the leaks first.
Frosted nail tips are condensation caught in the act — fix ventilation with the roof.
Dampproofing resists soil moisture; waterproofing holds back actual water pressure.
Backer rod sets the width-to-depth ratio so the bead stretches instead of tearing.
Without a kick-out, the roof's edge water pours straight into the wall assembly.
coatings: Silicone doesn't mind sitting water — it's the ponding-area chemistry.
Acrylics are water-based — standing water re-softens them.
Almost nothing sticks to cured silicone except more silicone.
Urethane takes traffic and impact — the walkway and hail layer.
Coverage specs exist to hit a dry-film thickness — thin mils are the classic failure.
Coatings restore sound roofs; prep and adhesion testing decide the outcome.
Coating over wet insulation seals the water in — scan, cut, and replace it first.
UV destroys bare foam — the topcoat with granules is SPF's armor.
Closed-cell SPF gives ~R-6+ per inch while sealing seamlessly.
repair: Water travels along framing and decking before it drips — the stain is the end of the trip.
Field shingles rarely leak — boots, flashings and valleys cause most calls.
Bottom-up zones isolate the entry point; flooding the roof tells you nothing.
Cement smears fail in a year and bury the detail a real repair needs.
Hail bruises are random dark hits with granule loss — sometimes a star-shaped mat fracture.
Soft metals dent honestly — clean gutters and vents mean be skeptical of the shingles.
A crease means the mat folded — the shingle is broken even lying flat.
The 10×10 square standardizes the count carriers use to total a slope.
Two layers is the code ceiling — over two, everything comes off.
Two layers, soft deck, or shakes underneath all force a tear-off by code or sense.
The savings up front cost deck visibility, service life and warranty coverage.
1/150 of attic area in net free vent area (1/300 balanced) is the code baseline.
Cool air in low at soffits, warm air out high at the ridge — that's the loop.
A fan near a ridge vent pulls air backwards through it — and weather comes along.
1/16"–1/8" per foot drains reliably while still reading level from the ground.
A 2"×3" downspout handles roughly 600 sq ft of roof — count them by area served.
estimating: The loaded rate adds taxes, comp and benefits — the real hourly cost of a roofer.
Your own job-cost history beats any book — it's your crews on your market's roofs.
Job-specific costs attach to THIS job — permits, dump fees, steep charges.
Published numbers don't know your crew or wages — adjust them with your data.
Boom delivery and staging cut crew-hours without cutting price — pure margin.
Overhead is the cost of existing — rent, trucks, insurance — recovered on every job.
Advertising and estimating time run whether or not this job sells — that's overhead.
At 10% margin, a 5% discount is half your profit handed away.
Two multipliers, in order: overhead recovery first, then profit on top.
Written unit prices make hidden rot a documented change, not a fight.
Winning everything means the market would have paid more — you're underpriced.
25–40% on qualified leads balances competitiveness against giveaway pricing.
